content: Chlamydiae is a bacterial phylum consisting of obligate intracellular pathogens. These bacteria are unable to survive or replicate outside of a eukaryotic host cell. Many species of Chlamydiae exist asymptomatically within specific hosts, which are thought to act as natural reservoirs for these organisms. Chlamydiae are as small as, or smaller than, many viruses. Within host cells, they adopt an intracellular replicative form, while outside the host cell, they exist in an extracellular infectious form. In laboratory settings, Chlamydiae can only be cultivated in environments where their host cells are present. This means they cannot be propagated in standard bacterial culture media and are most effectively isolated while still inside host cells. Cavalier-Smith has proposed that Chlamydiae belong to the clade Planctobacteria within the larger clade Gracilicutes. Historically, diseases resembling chlamydial infections of the eye were described in ancient Chinese and Egyptian texts. A modern description of Chlamydia-like organisms was provided by Halberstaedter and von Prowazek in 1907. In the late 1920s and early 1930s, chlamydial isolates were cultured in the yolk sacs of embryonating eggs during a human pneumonia outbreak. By the mid-20th century, isolates had been obtained from numerous vertebrate species. The term Chlamydia, derived from the Greek word for cloak, first appeared in the literature in 1945, although other names such as Bedsonia, Miyagawanella, ornithosis agents, TRIC agents, and PLT agents were also used. In 1966, Chlamydiae were formally recognized as bacteria, and the genus Chlamydia was validated. The Order Chlamydiales was established by Storz and Page in 1971. Between 1989 and 1999, new families, genera, and species within the phylum were identified. The phylum Chlamydiae was officially included in Bergey’s Manual of Systematic Bacteriology. By 2006, genetic data for over 350 chlamydial lineages had been reported, with four recognized families (Chlamydiaceae, Parachlamydiaceae, Simkaniaceae, and Waddliaceae) and one proposed family (Rhabdochlamydiaceae). Structurally, Chlamydiae can function as either parasites or endosymbionts, depending on the eukaryotic host and the specific chlamydial species. The elementary bodies (EBs), which are the infectious form, are approximately 0.3 μm in diameter and have a rigid cell wall stabilized by disulfide bonds. Reticulate bodies (RBs), the replicative form, are larger (approximately 0.5–1 μm), metabolically active, and capable of binary fission. Binary division may involve ring structures composed of a transient type of peptidoglycan. Using electron microscopy, both EBs and RBs can be observed during replication within intracellular inclusions. These inclusions do not undergo acidification or lysosomal fusion and are distinct from canonical endocytic vesicles, instead resembling recycling endosomes. After several days of replication, RBs transform back into metabolically inactive EBs, which are released from the host cell either through cell rupture or fusion of the inclusion and plasma membranes. Chlamydiae are transmitted via aerosols or direct contact and do not require an alternate vector for transmission. From a genomic perspective, Chlamydiae represent a unique bacterial evolutionary group that diverged from other bacteria approximately one billion years ago. There is some debate regarding their evolutionary relationship to other bacterial groups, such as Planctomycetales or Spirochaetes. Genome sequencing has revealed that 11% of the genes in Candidatus Protochlamydia amoebophila UWE25 and 4% of the genes in Chlamydiaceae are most similar to genes found in chloroplasts, plants, and cyanobacteria. Ribosomal RNA gene comparisons have provided a phylogeny of known strains within the phylum. The unique characteristics of Chlamydiae have facilitated the use of DNA-based diagnostics for identifying chlamydial infections. There are three primary species of Chlamydiae that commonly infect humans: 1. Chlamydia trachomatis, which causes the eye disease trachoma and the sexually transmitted infection chlamydia. 2. Chlamydophila pneumoniae, which is responsible for a form of pneumonia. 3. Chlamydophila psittaci, which causes psittacosis, a zoonotic disease often associated with birds.
